_comment: Digests for external kernels, pinned so that every fetch after the first is a CHECK rather
than a download. `farsight fetch kernel` requires --expect-sha256 and has no flag to skip
it; this file is where that value comes from.
READ THIS BEFORE ADDING A ROW. NAIF publishes no checksums for the generic kernels -- there
is no checksums.txt, no SHA256SUMS, and the directory readme carries no digest (verified
2026-09-07). So the FIRST acquisition of any kernel here could not verify anything: the
digest was obtained by downloading the file and hashing it. That is trust-on-first-use, and
it is a genuinely weaker property than the rest of this system provides -- it establishes
that everyone afterwards gets the same bytes we got, not that the bytes we got were the
bytes NAIF published. Recorded as DEV-16.
A row is added by fetching, hashing, and writing the result down. Changing an existing row
is not a maintenance action: a kernel's bytes do not change, so a differing digest means
either the publisher reissued the file under the same name or something is wrong, and both
need a human to look rather than an edit.

kernels.license_note: NAIF generic kernel; NASA/JPL public domain, redistributable unmodified.
note: The leapsecond kernel. ADR-016 decision 6 requires exactly one LSK per KernelSet, which
is what makes 'the pinned LSK' in ADR-015's conversion records denote a single kernel.
USE THE UNIX VARIANT ON EVERY PLATFORM. NAIF also publishes naif0012.tls.pc, which is
the same kernel with CRLF line endings and is 5409 bytes -- a DIFFERENT content address
for identical physics. SPICE reads both. Fetching the .pc variant on Windows would give
a design frozen there a different kernel_set_hash from one frozen on Linux, and ADR-006's
cross-platform golden would fail for a reason that has nothing to do with physics.
Do NOT pin latest_leapseconds.tls. It is a symlink NAIF updates in place, so the same URL
returns different bytes over time -- exactly what content addressing exists to prevent.
